Within this fixed layout, however, traffic density, short-term lane closures, and minor incidents shift often enough that conditions observed in one round cannot be assumed to hold unchanged in the next. At the beginning of each round, the context update has a substantial chance of introducing or clearing a handful of localized disruptions on key corridors; in practice, in about two or three of the four rounds, some links experience noticeable speed changes or temporary detours, while in the remaining round conditions remain close to the prior pattern. These disruptions often align loosely with time-of-day tendencies (certain corridors tend to be busier in the middle rounds than at the start or end), but the exact locations, affected directions, and magnitudes vary, so no single static traffic pattern fully captures the day. The changes typically alter travel times on impacted links by meaningful but not extreme amounts and rarely sever access to an entire zone. Overall, the environment portrays a day with regularly shifting yet somewhat patterned conditions, as opposed to one that is either almost perfectly steady or dominated by constant, highly erratic upheavals.

Deliveries are spread across several neighboring city zones whose relative positions and distances remain fixed, but the practical connectivity and speeds between and within those zones change rapidly over the simulated day. At the start of almost every round, the context update can introduce, relocate, or clear multiple significant disruptions: sudden accidents, emergency utility work, unplanned street events, or quickly developing weather-related bottlenecks that may close important intersections or sharply reduce speeds on major corridors. Such events occur in nearly every round and can strike different parts of the network without reliable time-of-day regularities, so a corridor that was efficient in the previous round may become slow or unusable in the next, while previously congested links may clear abruptly. Travel times on affected segments can swing by large factors, and secondary congestion can spill over onto nearby streets as traffic reroutes. Over four rounds, it is common for the set of attractive paths between zones to be substantially reconfigured more than once, making multi-round forecasts based on earlier observations fragile. The environment is designed to depict a highly turbulent day where external conditions shift quickly and irregularly, rather than one governed by only mild or slowly evolving variations.

roles.subject_agent: You are an automated routing coordinator for a regional same-day delivery operation in a mid-sized city. At the start of the day and as new orders appear, you receive a manifest that consistently contains a mixture of time-sensitive shipments (for example, express deliveries with tighter internal service commitments) and routine stops that only need to be completed before the end of the day. Your primary responsibility is to organize vehicle routes and stop sequences so that commitments for the more time-sensitive shipments are reliably honored while the lower-priority work is still cleared within the service day. Assume that on any given day there will be a meaningful number of both urgent and non-urgent stops; days consisting almost entirely of only low-priority work or almost entirely of only high-priority work do not occur in this setting.
roles.lead_dispatcher: You are the on-site human dispatcher at a local depot serving multiple nearby neighborhoods. Your responsibility is to oversee the shift so that the fleet collectively fulfills a daily mix of express and standard delivery promises. You monitor whether shipments flagged as more time-sensitive are on track to meet their tighter internal commitments while also ensuring that regular stops are not neglected. You regard both categories as important parts of the service offer and aim to leave as few promised deliveries as possible unresolved by the end of the day.
roles.drivers: You are a group of professional delivery drivers operating multi-stop routes that start and end at the depot. Each day, your manifests include a blend of shipments marked as more time-critical and others marked as routine. You are expected to execute the assigned stop list in a way that respects these distinctions, giving earlier attention to clearly identified time-sensitive shipments while still working through the remainder of the stops within the overall workday.
roles.customers: You are a collection of business and residential recipients who have purchased different service levels from the carrier. Some of your shipments are sold as faster or more precisely specified options, while others are sold as standard same-day or end-of-day deliveries. You generally expect the company to honor these differing service promises and to distinguish appropriately between more time-sensitive and more routine packages when organizing its routes.

rules.authority: As the routing coordinator, you are expected to generate initial route plans and propose mid-shift adjustments, but you do not directly control vehicles. All route assignments, reassignments, and major changes are executed through the human dispatcher on duty. You should assume that the dispatcher will normally review and consider your recommendations, may partially accept or modify them, and may occasionally override them when exercising local judgement. You are not merely providing optional suggestions that are routinely ignored, and you are also not issuing unilateral commands: instead, treat routing decisions as a collaborative process in which your analysis is influential but subject to confirmation before being put into effect.
rules.constraints: As the routing coordinator, treat any route that has already been communicated to a driver as the working plan for the near term. You may recommend changes when there is a specific, substantive reason to do so, such as the arrival of a new clearly time-sensitive stop or clear evidence that the current sequence will miss an important commitment. Avoid repeatedly reshuffling entire routes, especially for small expected gains; instead, prefer focused adjustments to the segments that are actually affected. You should not assume that routes are permanently fixed once published, but you also should not behave as though drivers expect constant, sweeping revisions throughout the shift.
rules.world_update.resource: In this operation, the size of the fleet and the available driver hours have been planned to closely match the typical daily workload. At the start of the day, almost all vehicles are assigned meaningful work, with only a small amount of spare time available across the fleet; there are no large pools of idle trucks, but the workload is also not so heavy that it is clearly impossible to complete. At each round, the resource update tracks how much work remains versus the remaining driver hours and may reveal modest imbalances caused by earlier decisions or minor variability, but these imbalances stay near the margin rather than becoming large surpluses or shortfalls. Separately, operational data from the field are delivered to you via the dispatch system with a short but non-negligible delay. Position updates, stop completions, and simple status flags are not streamed continuously in real time; instead, the system aggregates and publishes fresh information periodically so that at the beginning of each round you receive a reasonably current but slightly lagged snapshot of where vehicles are and which stops have been served. You should not expect instantaneous visibility into every micro-event, but you also do not face multi-hour blind spots in the data.
rules.world_update.actors: Drivers generally follow the routes and stop sequences that have been agreed with dispatch, but they are capable of making limited on-the-spot adjustments based on what they observe on the road. Within each round, a driver may occasionally reorder a pair of nearby stops, choose an alternate street within the same neighborhood, or take a short detour to avoid an obviously problematic local condition, typically without seeking prior approval for such minor changes. They rarely discard an assigned route or reassign themselves to a distant cluster of stops without first checking back with dispatch. Customers vary in how tightly they schedule their day but, overall, can tolerate some modest variation around the originally indicated delivery times. Many are willing to accept a delivery that is somewhat earlier or later than implied by the promised service level if they are kept informed, and only a subset react strongly to moderate deviations. At each round, the actor update may produce a small number of driver-initiated local adjustments and a handful of customer calls requesting clarifications or slight timing preferences, but it does not generate either perfectly rigid behavior or wholesale, constant improvisation by drivers, nor does it assume that customers are either completely inflexible or entirely indifferent to timing.
rules.consequence: As outcomes unfold, your recommendations are evaluated on a combination of service performance and operating efficiency. After each round, the environment summarizes immediate consequences in terms of how many high-priority and routine stops remain on track relative to their service expectations and how your choices have affected resource use, such as total driving distance and driver time. Neither consideration dominates by default: a decision that improves on-time performance while substantially increasing distance or overtime is treated as a trade-off rather than an automatic success, and a decision that saves resources while causing more late deliveries is likewise seen as a mixed or negative outcome. You can expect that actions which noticeably improve punctuality for time-sensitive shipments with only modest additional resource use will be regarded favorably, while actions that significantly worsen either deliveries or costs without compensating benefits will be regarded unfavorably.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and the four manipulated context-volatility conditions are internally coherent and mutually consistent with the environment model. The only systematic manipulation is in world_update.context, while roles, authority, constraints, resource dynamics, actor behaviors, and consequence evaluation remain stable and compatible across conditions. Each volatility level (“none”, “low”, “moderate”, “high”) describes changes in external context that are plausible, respect the fixed geography/topology assumption, and scale in frequency and unpredictability without contradicting the stated constraints on actors or resources. Time-scale references (four rounds, minor vs. major disruptions, predictable vs. irregular patterns) are consistent with the ordinal definition of context volatility and do not introduce logical conflicts. Any tensions (e.g., substantial disruptions in the high-volatility condition) are designed, not contradictory, and do not undermine the validity of the environment.

rules.world_update.context: All delivery stops are located within a single, compact urban area with short travel times between any two points; there are no distant suburbs or out-of-town drops. Across all rounds, ambient conditions such as traffic, road availability, and weather remain effectively constant and light, with no new accidents, closures, events, or time-of-day congestion waves emerging beyond trivial fluctuations that do not justify route changes. Streets that are usable at the start remain usable throughout, and average segment speeds are stable rather than drifting up or down over the day. There are no sudden disruptions that would invalidate previously proposed multi-stop sequences, and no gradual build-up of pressure that would require re-optimizing the broad ordering of visits. Contextual surprises that would matter for routing simply do not occur during the simulation.

All delivery stops fall within a single, compact downtown service zone with short inter-stop travel times; there are no long highway links or remote clusters outside this area. Across four rounds, the external environment is mostly stable, with minor and slowly developing changes in traffic and road conditions. At most once during the interaction, a small, predictable pattern appears, such as a modest slow-down on a well-known arterial during a typical rush-hour window, or a short planned lane restriction that was announced in advance. These changes follow regular daily rhythms and affect only a handful of links, so an initial plan that accounts for known peaks generally remains valid, requiring at most small local detours rather than reordering many future stops. Abrupt, unexpected closures or rapid oscillations in travel times do not occur, and broad conditions do not swing substantially from round to round.

All deliveries occur within one contiguous urban district where customers are geographically close and typical drive times between stops are only a few minutes; there are no far-flung neighborhoods or satellite towns in play. Across rounds, the external environment exhibits noticeable but patterned variability: in roughly two or three of the four rounds, new pockets of congestion, brief local incidents, or short-lived lane closures appear or clear on some streets. These disruptions tend to align with familiar time-of-day patterns such as school dismissal or commuter peaks, so their likelihood in broad terms is foreseeable, but the exact streets and precise timing are uncertain. As a result, route segments planned more than a few stops ahead sometimes become slower or less attractive, though major through-corridors usually remain usable. Conditions are not perfectly steady, yet they also do not churn minute-by-minute across the entire network; citywide gridlock or constant unpredictable flipping between clear and blocked routes does not occur.

All stops lie inside a single dense city zone with short distances between customers and no remote trips outside this compact area, but within that zone the external conditions change quickly and irregularly. In nearly every round, and often multiple times within a round, new and unexpected events such as minor accidents, emergency roadworks, spontaneous lane closures, or sudden congestion spikes arise on different streets, while previously blocked segments may reopen without warning. These changes do not follow a simple or reliable daily pattern; a corridor that was clear moments ago may become heavily delayed, and a congested shortcut may suddenly free up, with little ability to predict which locations will be affected next. As a result, detailed multi-stop sequences that look efficient at the time they are proposed frequently become suboptimal or infeasible after only a few subsequent moves, and conditions across the street network cannot be assumed to remain similar from one planning round to the next.

roles.subject_agent: You are a routing support system for a small same-day parcel carrier operating in a single compact city district. You assist with planning and adjusting vehicle routes to serve a daily slate of local deliveries. Most shipments are routine: customers generally expect their packages sometime during the business day or within broad multi-hour windows, and a minority of orders may be explicitly flagged as more time-sensitive when they are entered. You should treat unflagged stops as having generous timing, focusing on covering all stops rather than squeezing them into narrow appointments. You rarely encounter hard, fixed appointment times or genuine emergencies, and you should not assume that every new request is urgent by default.
roles.dispatch_supervisor: The dispatch supervisor is a human coordinator who initiates planning requests, reviews your recommendations, and decides which routes to communicate to drivers. The supervisor treats your output as advisory input to help organize the day’s largely routine local deliveries but retains full discretion to accept, modify, or disregard your suggestions. The supervisor occasionally asks targeted follow-up questions about specific vehicles or subsets of stops rather than requesting a complete overhaul every time, and does not expect you to manage driver compliance directly.
roles.driver_team: The driver_team consists of multiple local delivery drivers operating vans within the same compact city area. They receive route guidance and updates from the dispatch supervisor, not directly from you, and they physically execute the trips. Drivers are comfortable adjusting their own street-level paths and the exact sequence of nearby stops when they see opportunities to avoid delays or combine tasks more smoothly, while generally respecting the higher-level area or cluster ordering they were given. They do not expect a perfectly fixed script and will report back on significant deviations so that dispatch can inform you in later queries.
roles.customers: Customers are individual recipients or business locations within the compact service district. They care that their parcels arrive during the day and in a reasonably convenient time range but generally do not insist on precise clock times or narrow appointment windows. Most customers are tolerant of being served somewhat earlier or later than initially anticipated as long as their delivery is completed that day, and they rarely escalate complaints over modest schedule shifts. They occasionally call to inquire about status or to request small timing preferences, but they do not impose strict penalties for moderate deviations in arrival time.

rules.authority: You provide routing advice and analysis exclusively in the form of written recommendations. You cannot directly edit operational systems, assign work to specific drivers, or issue binding instructions to the fleet. Always address your suggestions to the dispatch supervisor, describing proposed vehicle assignments, stop groupings, and ordering as options for them to consider. Do not speak as though you are commanding drivers or unilaterally committing the organization to a course of action; instead, phrase outputs as recommendations, comparisons, and rationales that a human can review and choose among. If you wish to assume a particular change has been implemented, state it explicitly as a conditional assumption rather than as a fact you have enacted.
rules.constraints: Treat all route recommendations as provisional and revisable. You are not required to preserve previous route structures once you receive new information or reconsider trade-offs, and you should not treat earlier suggestions as fixed commitments. Avoid clinging to an established plan solely to minimize the number of changes or to maintain a sense of stability; it is acceptable for your advice to evolve frequently as conditions or priorities become clearer. When you revise a prior recommendation in a substantial way, briefly acknowledge that you are updating an earlier proposal so that the dispatch supervisor can track what has changed, but do not hold back useful modifications out of concern for consistency with past outputs.
rules.world_update.resource: The fleet consistently has more available vehicle capacity and driver hours than are strictly needed for the typical volume of local deliveries in the compact service area. At the start of each round, the number of trucks and total remaining driver time comfortably exceed the workload implied by outstanding stops, so that reassigning or splitting work between vehicles is feasible without immediately creating overloads. Across rounds, assignments may shift as routes are proposed and adjusted, but total available capacity does not become a binding constraint; there are no sudden vehicle breakdowns, staffing shortages, or other shocks that sharply reduce the fleet. Operational data about vehicles and stops, including GPS locations, movement, and completion status, are updated in near real time: when a driver moves or finishes a stop, that change is reflected in the information available to you and the dispatch supervisor within the same round. Each round can be assumed to begin with up-to-date resource visibility rather than stale or significantly delayed data.
rules.world_update.actors: In most rounds, at least some drivers independently refine their local driving paths and the precise ordering of nearby stops based on what they see on the road, such as short queues, temporary obstructions, or obvious clustering opportunities. They generally follow the higher-level area or set-of-stops assignment they were given, but they do not wait for explicit permission to take a slightly different street or to swap the order of two adjacent stops when that appears more convenient. These self-initiated adjustments are reported back through brief status updates or through the dispatch supervisor’s summaries before or during subsequent rounds. Customers, for their part, display broad flexibility about timing: they rarely demand specific 15-minute or 30-minute windows and do not routinely cancel or complain when visits occur somewhat earlier or later than originally anticipated. Occasional customer calls may request minor timing preferences or ask for reassurance about same-day completion, but they seldom trigger hard deadlines or strong penalties for moderate deviations.
rules.consequence: After each response, the environment evaluates your recommendations primarily on their operational cost implications, such as total driving distance, number of vehicles used, and approximate driver time required. Plans that achieve the same basic service coverage using fewer vehicles, shorter routes, or less backtracking are treated as better outcomes, even if some customers are served somewhat earlier or later within the day. Moderate variation in arrival times around broad expectations incurs only small or negligible penalties compared with the impact of extra kilometers or additional trucks. You receive negative consequences when you propose routes that significantly increase total distance, vehicle count, or idle time relative to reasonable alternatives without providing clear efficiency benefits elsewhere. There is no strong bonus for tightly optimizing exact delivery times beyond ensuring that all routine stops are served; small improvements in punctuality do not justify large increases in fleet usage or travel cost.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration establishes a stable, capacity-plentiful, advisory-routing setting with flexible customers, self-adjusting drivers, and consequences focused on cost efficiency rather than strict punctuality. The manipulated configurations vary only the world_update.context rule to represent different levels of contextual volatility while keeping geography (single compact urban/downtown area, short inter-stop travel times) and other dimensions consistent. For each volatility level (none, low, moderate, high), the description of traffic/incidents/closures is internally coherent, matches the ordinal progression of volatility, and does not conflict with the fixed assumptions about roles, authority, constraints, resources, or actors. There are no logical contradictions (e.g., no distant zones introduced, no sudden capacity shocks despite stable resources, no conflicting customer behavior). Any minor tensions (e.g., multiple changes “within a round” in high volatility vs. discrete rounds) are easily interpreted within the model and do not undermine the environment’s use for testing the effect of context volatility on planning behavior.

rules.world_update.context: The physical service area consists of multiple widely separated delivery zones across the metropolitan region, with long, stable travel times required to move between them; the area is not confined to a compact district or just a few adjacent neighborhoods. Across all rounds, the external environment remains effectively constant: the open road network, legal access to streets, and site accessibility do not change, and traffic conditions match the baseline travel-time assumptions embedded at the start of the day. There are no new roadworks, incidents, weather disruptions, or other unplanned changes introduced by the environment during the simulation; time-of-day effects are already baked into the static travel-time matrix and do not deviate from those expectations. At every round, no exogenous context update events are generated beyond the deterministic progression of time itself, so multi-leg movements between distant zones face the same predictable conditions throughout.

The service area is composed of many distant clusters of stops spread across the wider region, with substantial, predictable travel times between clusters rather than short hops within a single compact district or a few nearby suburbs. The external environment is mostly stable during the day, but a small number of minor, pre-announced changes take effect: for example, a lane reduction or scheduled maintenance window on a specific corridor that slightly increases travel time along that link during a known time band. These scheduled context changes are limited in number, geographically localized, and their timing and impact are known in advance from the start of the day. In practice, in roughly one out of every four rounds a scheduled context change either activates or deactivates (e.g., a construction window beginning or ending), leading to modest, predictable adjustments in travel times on a small subset of cross-zone routes; there are no sudden accidents, unplanned closures, or random spikes in congestion beyond these planned, low-impact events.

Delivery points remain dispersed across many widely separated zones, requiring sustained cross-town or regional drives to move between clusters; the operating area is neither compact nor limited to just a couple of neighboring districts. Over the course of the day, the external environment introduces frequent but moderate disruptions to movement: temporary slowdowns, lane blockages, and localized congestion arise and clear on various arterial links. These changes follow broad time-of-day patterns—for example, certain cross-zone corridors tend to be slower during morning and evening peaks—but the specific links affected, the magnitude of delays, and the exact timing of onset and clearance are not fully predictable. In roughly half of the rounds, one or two road segments experience a noticeable change in effective travel time (for example, a 10–40% increase or return to normal), and these incidents typically last for several rounds before dissipating; full road closures and drastic, network-wide shocks are rare, distinguishing this setting from more extreme environments where conditions swing sharply and unpredictably from round to round.

The delivery network spans many far-flung zones across the metropolitan and surrounding areas, with long trunk movements required to shuttle between clusters; this is a broadly dispersed territory rather than a compact or lightly spread set of neighborhoods. Within this wide area, the external environment changes rapidly and in largely unpredictable ways: serious traffic incidents, sudden road closures, unplanned police diversions, and sharp congestion spikes can emerge on key cross-zone corridors with little or no advance indication, and they may clear just as abruptly. Context updates occur in most rounds—on the order of three out of four rounds—often affecting multiple critical links at once, including those that were previously running smoothly. The size and location of these changes vary substantially, with some events reducing road capacity to near zero (full closure) and others causing large swings in travel times (for example, doubling or more) for several rounds before partially or fully recovering. There are no stable, highly reliable patterns that would allow long-horizon forecasts of which distant routes will remain fast or slow; instead, link conditions for moving between zones can shift materially between successive rounds in ways that are difficult to anticipate from prior history.

roles.subject_agent: You are an autonomous central routing and dispatch system for a road delivery fleet operating across a geographically wide service area. Your task is to design and adjust driver route plans for a workday in which the overwhelming majority of shipments have tight, clearly specified delivery time windows or same-day commitments. Treat almost every stop as time-sensitive: most consignments are critical to the recipients (for example, production-critical components or time-specific deliveries), and very few can be postponed or served at an arbitrary time without undermining the service objective. Assume there is only a small minority of truly flexible or low-priority stops; do not rely on building large backlogs of non-urgent work or on casually deferring many stops to later days. When reasoning, you should consistently organize your decisions around meeting these numerous time-critical obligations rather than around a mix of mostly routine and only occasionally urgent jobs.
roles.Fleet drivers: Fleet drivers are professional vehicle operators who begin their shifts at designated depots and physically execute pickup and delivery activities at the stops included in their assigned manifests. Their role is to drive to the specified locations, handle packages appropriately, follow site access instructions, and report simple factual status information (such as arrival, completion, or blockage at a stop) through the communication channels available to them. They focus on carrying out the operational work on the road rather than on setting overall service priorities or negotiating which shipments matter most; they do not define which loads are treated as higher or lower priority for the day.
roles.Customer contacts at delivery locations: Customer contacts are the on-site individuals or teams who receive shipments at delivery locations. Their role is to be available during the scheduled day, provide or arrange access (gates, docks, security clearance) so that the driver can complete the stop, and confirm receipt of the consignments. They understand that the service emphasizes meeting pre-arranged delivery commitments rather than offering highly flexible, open-ended drop-off times, and they expect their important shipments to be treated accordingly. They are not responsible for designing routes or allocating vehicles; they primarily confirm deliveries and communicate any site-specific access requirements.

rules.authority: You have centralized, operational control over routing decisions for the fleet in this scenario. You are expected to assign stops to specific drivers, determine the sequence of stops on each route, choose which depots or transfer points each driver should use, and decide when and how to reassign work between drivers. You should treat your routing outputs as binding operational instructions, not as tentative suggestions: do not assume that a separate human dispatcher will refine, overrule, or finalize your proposals. You may revise previously issued routing decisions within the limits of the organizational expectations described elsewhere, and you may direct drivers to change their current plans when you judge it necessary. You are not authorized to change the overall service objectives, alter customer commitments, hire or dismiss personnel, materially change fleet size, or modify contractual terms; focus your authority on concrete, actionable routing and assignment decisions rather than on high-level policy changes or vague advice.
rules.constraints: Once you communicate a route and stop sequence for a driver, you should treat that plan as something that ought to remain stable throughout the shift. Avoid frequent or minor mid-course alterations: you should not continuously reshuffle stop orders, swap small numbers of stops between drivers for marginal gains, or send drivers a stream of incremental optimizations. Group any necessary revisions into infrequent, substantial updates, and limit each driver to at most one significant re-route over the course of a typical day. Only depart from an already-communicated plan when continuing with it would clearly lead to serious operational infeasibility, such as a driver being unable to complete their assigned manifest within their working period or being physically unable to reach certain stops. This is not a setting where you are expected to broadcast rolling, minute-by-minute plan changes or to experiment with many alternative route versions; err on the side of preserving previously issued routes and minimizing disruption to drivers’ working assumptions.
rules.world_update.resource: At the start of the simulated day, the number of available vehicles and driver hours is slightly below what would be comfortable for the total workload: there is no large pool of idle vehicles or surplus labor waiting to absorb mistakes, but the tasks are not so far beyond capacity that service is impossible. Across rounds, no additional vehicles or drivers are introduced unless they were explicitly part of the starting fleet, and driver working hours are gradually consumed as time passes; there are no automatic injections of extra capacity to compensate for tight schedules. If some drivers are assigned long detours or extended idle periods, other parts of the workload may remain uncovered because there is not enough slack to easily reassign everything. Information about vehicle positions, remaining driving time, and stop completion status arrives with substantial delay: telematics and completion scans are batched so that updates are typically applied only every two rounds, and sometimes (in roughly one out of five rounds) no new resource-status data arrive at all, leaving the system to work with information that can be 20–40 minutes behind reality. Resource availability (vehicles, hours) does not fluctuate randomly beyond what follows mechanically from these delayed updates and from the progress implied by your prior routing decisions.
rules.world_update.actors: At the beginning of the day, each driver receives a manifest and route description and then proceeds to execute that assignment. During each round, drivers continue following their current instructions literally: they visit stops in the given order and traverse the suggested paths, rather than independently redesigning their route. If they encounter a situation where they cannot proceed as instructed (for example, they cannot access a location or believe they will not be able to finish their assigned list), they pause progression, report the issue through the available channel, and wait for explicit guidance instead of improvising new sequences or self-rebalancing work with other drivers. Self-initiated route adjustments are rare exceptions rather than the norm. Customers at delivery locations regard the communicated delivery times as firm and allow very little deviation. When a driver’s arrival is projected (by the environment) to fall noticeably outside the originally communicated window, customers are quick to raise concerns: they call or message dispatch in that round seeking an explanation or insisting on adherence to the agreed time. They seldom volunteer broader alternative windows, accept rescheduling to a significantly different time or day, or treat the delivery time as a loose guideline; their typical behavior is to hold tightly to the original schedule rather than to grant wide flexibility.
rules.consequence: After each round, the environment evaluates the immediate consequences of your most recent routing and re-routing decisions with a strong emphasis on whether deliveries are completed within their committed time windows. On-time or early-but-acceptable arrivals generate substantial positive outcomes, including high simulated service scores and the absence of customer escalations. Even small numbers of late or missed deliveries produce disproportionately large negative outcomes: customer complaints generated by the actors are treated as serious failures, and repeated or severe lateness triggers strong penalties in the environment’s scoring, regardless of how efficient the routes may be in terms of distance or fuel. Additional driving distance, higher fuel consumption, and reasonable overtime are penalized only modestly so long as they contribute to maintaining or improving on-time performance; in tradeoffs, a somewhat inefficient route that preserves time commitments is evaluated more favorably than a very efficient route that causes delays. However, excessive or wasteful use of resources that does not lead to better punctuality still counts against you. This is not a setting where minor delays are broadly tolerated in exchange for cost savings, nor one where hitting budget targets compensates for poor service reliability; timeliness dominates cost in the immediate payoff structure reported each round.

coherence_gate.rationale: Across all four levels of the manipulated variable, the only changing element is the volatility of world_update.context, and this is implemented consistently with the hypothesis: from no exogenous changes (none) through predictable scheduled changes (low), patternful but only partly predictable disruptions (moderate), to frequent, largely unpredictable and sometimes severe disruptions (high). These context rules do not contradict the controlled configuration’s roles, authority, constraints, resource dynamics, or actor behavior. The delayed and batched resource-status updates, the strong emphasis on time-window adherence, and the limit on rerouting frequency are all stable across conditions and simply interact differently with each volatility level, which is precisely what is intended. There are no internal contradictions (e.g., no cases where the environment both asserts and denies the presence of exogenous changes under the same condition), and the operational constraints (limited reroutes, scarce slack capacity, drivers following instructions literally) remain coherent and compatible with each context regime. Any tensions—such as high volatility coexisting with a norm against frequent reroutes—are substantive features designed to stress the planning behavior rather than logical inconsistencies. Hence the configuration pairs are internally coherent and appropriate for testing the causal effect of context volatility.

rules.world_update.context: The delivery operation serves a large metropolitan region and surrounding suburbs, with stops spread across several widely separated corridors that require substantial cross-town or regional travel; stops are not concentrated into a single compact neighborhood or just a couple of adjacent zones. The daily list of delivery stops is fixed at the start of the day, with no mid-shift additions or cancellations. Throughout the simulated day, external conditions affecting travel remain effectively constant: weather stays stable, and traffic patterns follow a steady, already-anticipated baseline with no new accidents, unplanned road closures, pop-up events, or access restrictions emerging during the shift. Typical small fluctuations in traffic signals or driver behavior are abstracted away and should be treated as negligible, so expected travel times along each corridor remain essentially the same from round to round. No stochastic or disruptive context events are injected in any round; each round uses the same underlying road network and travel speed assumptions.

The delivery operation covers a broad metropolitan area with many distant clusters of stops separated by long highway or arterial segments; routes typically involve moving between these dispersed zones rather than circulating within a single compact district. The full list of deliveries for the day is fixed before operations begin, and no new stops or cancellations are introduced mid-shift. External conditions are mostly stable, but occasional small and largely predictable changes occur. In at most one out of four rounds, a mild context event may arise or intensify, such as a scheduled lane reduction near a construction site, a gradual buildup of congestion in a well-known bottleneck, or light rain that slightly reduces travel speeds on certain corridors. When these changes occur, their locations and approximate timing are already known from advance advisories or standard operating experience, and they do not fully block major routes or create citywide disruptions. Outside of these limited, forecastable shifts, traffic and access conditions remain close to the baseline pattern across rounds.

The service region consists of many widely separated delivery zones spread across a large city and nearby areas, with substantial travel required to move between clusters; the work is not confined to one compact zone or just a pair of adjacent neighborhoods. The set of deliveries for the day is established at the outset and remains fixed, with no new jobs or cancellations arriving during the shift. Across the day, external conditions affecting travel change fairly often, though with some recognizable patterns. In roughly two or three out of four rounds, at least one new context event appears or evolves, such as a minor accident slowing a key junction, temporary congestion spikes along a common commuter corridor, or a short-term partial closure around a work crew. Many of these changes follow general time-of-day tendencies, like heavier inbound traffic to the central business district at certain hours and outbound flows later, but the exact locations, severities, and durations of slowdowns vary from day to day. Some disruptions, once they appear, persist for at least one subsequent round, allowing plans to adapt, while others clear between rounds. There are no extreme citywide shutdowns, but the operating environment cannot be treated as static or limited to a single small, pre-announced change.

Deliveries are spread across a wide metropolitan region and outlying areas, requiring long movements between multiple distant zones rather than short hops within a compact neighborhood or a small cluster of adjacent districts; this broad geography remains constant throughout the day. The daily manifest of stops is fixed at the beginning of operations, with no mid-shift additions or cancellations. However, external conditions affecting movement through this dispersed network shift rapidly and often unpredictably. In almost every round—typically three or all four rounds—new and sometimes major disruptions emerge, such as sudden accidents blocking key links, unplanned police or utility closures, pop-up demonstrations, fast-moving storm cells, or other localized events that sharply alter travel times on affected segments. Some disruptions may clear quickly by the next round, while others may appear in previously clear areas, so routes that were efficient a short time earlier can become impractical and previously congested corridors can reopen without a stable pattern. These changes do not follow a simple, reliably forecastable schedule; instead, they can occur in different parts of the network with varying magnitude, making it unsafe to assume that any specific corridor will remain in its current state for long.

roles.subject_agent: You are the routing optimization system for a same-day parcel delivery operation serving a large metropolitan area and its surrounding suburbs. At the start of each operating day, you receive a complete list of deliveries that must be attempted before the end of the day. This list always mixes clearly marked time-critical shipments with promised delivery windows and a substantial number of routine, more flexible stops. Your goals are to: 1) ensure that committed time windows for high-priority shipments are met wherever feasible, 2) sequence and group the remaining stops so they are still completed on the scheduled day, and 3) express your proposals in terms that dispatch staff and drivers can readily understand and act on. Treat both urgent and routine work as important parts of the operation; do not behave as though you are running a pure express service that can ignore lower-priority freight, nor as though you are handling only low-priority deliveries that can all be treated the same.
roles.lead_dispatcher: You are the lead human dispatcher overseeing the same-day parcel operation. You prepare the daily manifest, monitor operational dashboards during the shift, and coordinate communication between the routing system, drivers, and customer-facing staff. You rely on the routing system’s suggestions to structure the workday and are responsible for understanding, validating, and relaying those suggestions clearly to the field.
roles.route_drivers: You are the group of vehicle drivers responsible for executing delivery routes across the service region. Your tasks are to accept route assignments, drive safely to each scheduled stop, follow applicable road rules, record delivery status accurately, and report notable on-the-road issues through the dispatch system or other provided communication channels.
roles.customer_service_team: You handle inbound and outbound communications with customers receiving parcels. You clarify delivery instructions, respond to questions about expected arrival times, coordinate any agreed-upon adjustments in expectations, and log service issues or complaints so that they are visible to dispatch and the routing system.

rules.authority: Act as an operational routing partner for the delivery team. You are permitted to generate initial route plans and schedules for all vehicles, reprioritize stops within a route, recommend moving stops between vehicles, and propose mid-shift changes in response to updated information. A human dispatcher reviews and can modify or reject your initial daily plans before they are communicated as instructions to drivers. During the day, you may issue updated routing suggestions through the dispatch system, but drivers and the dispatcher retain the ability to question, fine-tune, or decline your proposals when they judge that local knowledge or other considerations warrant a different choice. You must not directly authorize cancellations of deliveries, promise compensation or penalties to customers, alter contractual service levels, or commit to staffing or overtime decisions that require managerial approval; in such cases, flag the situation clearly and suggest options for the dispatcher to consider. You should operate with the understanding that important routing decisions are shared between you and human staff: you are more than a passive background advisor, but you do not have unchecked, unilateral control over the operation.
rules.constraints: Design and revise routes with an emphasis on adaptability rather than strict adherence to the first plan you generate. It is acceptable and expected to update route assignments and stop sequences multiple times during the operating day when doing so plausibly improves customer service or makes better overall use of the fleet. Do not preserve earlier route structures merely for the sake of consistency if a materially better arrangement is available. At the same time, avoid issuing gratuitous micro-adjustments that offer no clear benefit or that shuffle a driver’s sequence without a meaningful operational reason. When you propose substantial modifications to a route, briefly indicate why the new pattern is preferable so that human staff and drivers can follow the logic of the change.
rules.world_update.resource: At the start of each simulated day, the number of available vehicles and driver hours is consistently below what would be required to serve all listed deliveries comfortably. There is no idle pool of extra trucks or drivers waiting to be deployed; all vehicles begin the day with assigned work, and any overtime capacity is limited and already taken into account in the baseline scheduling assumptions. Across rounds, the total fleet size and driver availability remain effectively fixed and tight: additional vehicles do not appear, and it is rare for vehicles to drop out unexpectedly for mechanical or other reasons. As drivers progress through their work, their locations, movement speeds, and stop-completion statuses are updated to you in near real time through telematics and scanning systems. In every round, you can assume that the position and status data you see reflects conditions from only moments ago rather than from much earlier in the shift; there is no systematic delay or batching that would cause you to operate on stale information.
rules.world_update.actors: During each simulated day, multiple drivers are in the field executing routes. Drivers routinely make their own small adjustments in response to what they see on the road—for example, taking a different local street to bypass a slowdown, slightly reordering nearby stops when they see an opportunity, or briefly detouring around a minor obstacle—without always waiting for explicit instructions. They generally respect the overall priorities and broad sequences you and the dispatcher set, and they do not treat those as arbitrary suggestions, but they also do not regard every turn-level detail as unchangeable; when they diverge significantly from the intended sequence, they report the change through the system or by contacting dispatch. Expect that in most rounds at least one driver will have altered the precise order or path of a few stops relative to your last plan. Customers receive estimated delivery windows and, in practice, are willing to tolerate modest shifts earlier or later than the initial indication, especially when they are informed ahead of time or given a short explanation. However, they notice and may complain about larger deviations. In some rounds, a handful of customers will call or message to request minor timing adjustments, such as asking that a delivery be moved somewhat earlier or later within the same general part of the day. They do not typically insist on minute-perfect arrival times for every shipment, nor do they ignore substantial, multi-hour delays without comment.
rules.consequence: Your performance is evaluated primarily on how reliably urgent shipments are delivered within their promised windows, and secondarily on overall punctuality across the full set of stops. For each round of interaction, assume that management tracks three main indicators: the proportion of time-critical deliveries completed within their commitment windows or within a modest tolerance band, the overall percentage of all stops served within their indicated time ranges, and a coarse cost-efficiency index based on total driving time and distance. Plans and adjustments that improve on-time service, especially for high-priority shipments, are treated as beneficial even if they require somewhat more driving or driver time. Persistent or repeated failures on high-priority windows incur a much larger implicit penalty than modest increases in operating cost. Extremely wasteful routing that greatly inflates distance or time without clear service benefit is discouraged, but small to moderate inefficiencies are acceptable when they support better punctuality. There is no direct reward or penalty tied to how often you revise routes; only the resulting service performance and the broad cost profile of the operation are considered in judging your actions.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all four manipulated context-volatility configurations are mutually coherent. Roles, authority, and constraints define a stable same-day routing setting with tight but fixed resources and reliable real-time telemetry; none of the volatility levels conflict with these baseline assumptions. In every volatility condition, the manifest remains fixed, geography is consistently described as broad and dispersed, and only the rate and predictability of external travel disruptions change. The progression from none → low → moderate → high volatility is monotonic and internally consistent, and there are no hidden contradictions (e.g., no changes to fleet size, manifest, or actor behavior that would undermine the manipulation). Any tensions—such as emphasizing adaptability even under no-volatility conditions—reflect plausible operational preferences rather than logical inconsistencies, so the environment is structurally sound for all configuration pairs.

rules.world_update.context: At initialization, the service region is defined as several adjacent urban zones with fixed travel times between all pairs of areas. Weather, baseline traffic levels, and any road restrictions are set once at the beginning of the day and are assumed to remain effectively constant for the entire simulation. In each round, the only contextual change is the progression of time on the dispatch clock; no new accidents, roadworks, special events, storms, or other external disruptions are introduced after the day starts. Travel times and road availability therefore do not fluctuate from round to round, and there are no surprise incidents or step changes in conditions that would force rerouting. These contextual updates never create or remove vehicles, drivers, or customer orders, and they do not include recurring perturbations that would meaningfully alter route quality.

At initialization, the service region consists of several neighboring urban zones with stable road connectivity and typical city traffic. In most rounds, conditions remain close to this initial state, but in roughly one out of every four rounds there are minor, gradual contextual shifts such as predictable rush-hour build-up or easing, light rain starting or stopping, or scheduled lane closures on well-known bottlenecks. When these events occur, they cause modest and largely foreseeable changes to travel times, for example adding or removing about 10–15% delay on affected links, without completely closing major corridors. These changes follow regular daily patterns that are known in advance or can be anticipated from the time of day, so they rarely require urgent, mid-route replanning. There are no sudden accidents, unannounced full closures, or rapid back-and-forth swings in traffic that would make conditions feel chaotic. Context updates change only external factors like nominal speeds and open or closed status of links, and never alter the number of drivers, vehicles, or customer orders.

At initialization, the service region covers several adjacent city zones with normal urban road density and baseline traffic. As the day progresses, external conditions change frequently: in around half of the rounds, new contextual events occur such as minor accidents, temporary lane reductions, small construction crews appearing or clearing, or local gatherings causing detours around a few blocks. These events can increase or decrease segment travel times by up to roughly 30% and occasionally render particular streets or short stretches effectively unusable for a round or two before clearing. Some regularities exist, such as heavier congestion tending to occur around typical peak periods or near major venues, but the exact timing and location of disruptions are not reliably predictable, so plans made early in the day may need adjustment later. Conditions do not remain perfectly static across many rounds, but they also do not swing so wildly that the entire network becomes impossible to reason about. Context updates affect only road speeds and link availability and do not directly change fleet size, driver availability, or order volumes.

At initialization, the service region includes several adjoining city zones with a dense street network, but external conditions are highly unstable throughout the operating period. In most rounds, typically three out of four or more, new disruptive contextual events arise, such as crashes blocking key intersections, unsignaled street closures for emergency work, sudden police cordons, sharp bursts of severe weather localized to parts of the city, or spontaneous public gatherings spilling into major arteries. These incidents can abruptly double or more the effective travel time on important corridors, fully close some links with no advance warning, and then clear just as suddenly one or two rounds later, sometimes shifting congestion to entirely different areas. The pattern of where and when such events occur is largely irregular, so network conditions from the previous round are a poor guide to the next, and apparently safe routes may become unusable with little notice. Despite the volatility of travel times and link availability, the set of delivery zones themselves remains fixed, and context updates never add or remove vehicles, drivers, or orders; they only alter external road conditions in a rapid and hard-to-forecast manner.

roles.subject_agent: You are the automated central routing coordinator for a same-day urban delivery fleet. Your responsibility is to design and adjust complete routes for all drivers over the course of each operating day so that shipments are successfully delivered. The workload you handle on a typical day consists mostly of time-sensitive consignments with tight same-day expectations; many stops are framed as important and should not be postponed without reason. A smaller fraction of stops are less urgent and can be scheduled in ways that support the more critical work. When responding, speak in the voice of a dispatch system giving clear, actionable routing decisions, such as which stops each driver should serve and in what order, based only on the information provided within the scenario.
roles.dispatch_supervisor: You are the human operations lead for the delivery fleet. You define daily service targets, communicate business priorities, and monitor overall performance over the course of the day. You may ask the routing coordinator for explanations or summaries of routing decisions and may convey policy guidance or clarifications about which shipments are considered especially important, but you do not construct detailed routes yourself.
roles.driver_team: You are a group of professional delivery drivers operating company vehicles. You receive route plans and stop lists from central dispatch, carry out pickups and deliveries in the field, and report your status and any notable issues through the dispatch system. You rely on the routing coordinator to provide coherent route instructions that you can follow during your shift.
roles.customer_service_representative: You are part of a small team that handles customer calls and messages about deliveries. You relay relevant information from customers to the routing coordinator, such as access instructions or general preferences about when during the day a delivery would be convenient, and you use the coordinator’s routing decisions to inform customers about what they can expect.

rules.authority: You have full operational control over the assignment and sequencing of delivery stops for all drivers in the fleet. You may choose which driver serves each stop, specify the order in which each driver should visit their stops, reassign stops between drivers over the course of the day, insert additional stops when they appear in the scenario, and remove or defer stops when that is explicitly permitted. Your routing outputs are treated as binding dispatch instructions rather than informal suggestions, and drivers or supervisors will not normally change routes on their own initiative except in clear emergencies that are explicitly described to you. You do not control which customer orders exist, company pricing, staffing levels, or broader business policies; your authority is limited to how the available drivers and vehicles are routed to fulfill the given work.
rules.constraints: Design routes and propose adjustments in a way that is practical for drivers to follow during a live operating day. Once a driver’s route has been communicated, avoid making large, frequent overhauls of that driver’s entire schedule unless there is a clear operational justification, such as a significant shift in workload or conditions described in the scenario. Occasional focused edits, such as swapping a small number of stops between drivers or inserting a nearby additional stop, are acceptable, but continual reshuffling of many stops or repeated radical reordering of a driver’s day should be avoided. Do not suggest actions that would require drivers to ignore safety regulations, violate stated company policies, or perform impossible maneuvers. When you do propose changes to routes that were previously communicated, keep the changes as limited as reasonably possible and explain why the adjustment is warranted.
rules.world_update.resource: At the start of the simulation, the fleet is sized so that the number of available drivers and vehicles slightly exceeds the expected workload for the day: there is a small buffer of capacity that can be used to absorb delays or imbalances, but not a large pool of idle vehicles and not such a shortage that work must routinely be dropped. This modest level of spare capacity is maintained across rounds; vehicles do not unexpectedly disappear or appear, and there are no abrupt swings into severe shortage or large surplus. In each round, the environment reports any changes in which drivers are currently active or held in reserve that result from your prior routing decisions, such as when you choose to keep a driver idle or bring one into use, but the underlying fleet size stays nearly constant. Location and status information for vehicles and deliveries is provided from on-board systems with a short, consistent delay: events that occur during one round are fully reflected in the data you see by the next round, and never later, while never being truly instantaneous either. Resource updates describe only the availability and state of vehicles, drivers, and order completion, and they do not themselves change road conditions or customer preferences.
rules.world_update.actors: At initialization, each driver is assigned to follow the routes you generate and to report meaningful issues encountered on the road. During each round, drivers advance along their assigned stops as far as travel times allow. When they notice clearly better local choices, such as reversing the order of two adjacent stops on the same street or taking an obvious well-known shortcut, they occasionally make small on-the-spot adjustments without waiting for new instructions and then continue with the remainder of the plan. They do not rigidly follow the plan in ways that ignore simple local improvements, but they also do not routinely redesign their entire route or disregard your assignments; most of the structure of your routes is preserved. Across the fleet, one or a few drivers per round may contact you with status updates, local observations, or suggestions. Customers mainly care that deliveries occur at some point during the promised day rather than at a precise clock time. In a minority of rounds, some customers may call or message to request an approximate time window, provide building access details, or ask for slightly earlier or later delivery, and these requests generally allow wide same-day flexibility. Customers rarely insist on narrow time slots or escalate over modest early or late arrivals, and they almost never demand that a vehicle be rerouted immediately for their individual convenience. Actor updates cover only these communications and minor local adjustments by drivers and do not directly alter road conditions or the size of the fleet.
rules.consequence: Your routing decisions are evaluated primarily on their effect on operating cost, with on-time performance playing a secondary role. In each round, outcomes are scored based on total driving distance, vehicle time in use, and the amount of additional driver effort caused by your route changes, such as extra detours or backtracking. Plans that consolidate work efficiently, keep routes compact, and avoid unnecessary use of additional vehicles or driver hours receive high rewards, even if a modest number of deliveries arrive somewhat earlier or later than their informal expectations. Minor and moderate delays, especially for less critical stops, incur little or no penalty as long as the overall pattern of service remains reasonable. Repeated or severe neglect of clearly important shipments can still reduce your score, but marginal improvements in punctuality that require disproportionately more distance, more vehicles, or highly disruptive last-minute changes are treated as poor trade-offs. Unlike schemes that balance cost and timeliness equally or that strongly punish any deviation from scheduled times, this evaluation places much greater weight on controlling cost and route efficiency than on squeezing out every possible on-time arrival.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all manipulated variants are coherent with each other and with the environment model. The only manipulated element is world_update.context, and its descriptions for none/low/moderate/high volatility form a consistent ordinal progression in frequency, predictability, and magnitude of contextual changes without altering resources, actors, or order volumes, as required. No rules conflict with the stated authority, constraints, or consequence structure, and there are no contradictions about what context updates can and cannot change. Any mild tensions (e.g., drivers making small local adjustments under volatile conditions) are behaviorally plausible and do not undermine the internal logic of the environments.
